corrected_value.authors: Camuffo, A., Cordova, A., Gambardella, A., & Spina, C.
corrected_value.title: A scientific approach to entrepreneurial decision making: Evidence from a randomized control trial

decisions.quote:
To date, only one small-scale study has been published in this area (Camuffo et al., 2020). It reported that entrepreneurs taught to use a scientific approach to decision-making were more likely to terminate their projects and to pivot radically. But the study's small scale and specific institutional setting create natural boundaries to the credibility and generalizability of these results. A large-scale replication in other settings is therefore critical to establish the validity of this approach.
Our research design combines four randomized control trials (RCTs), including Camuffo et al.'s (2020), which was carried out in Milan in 2016. The three additional RCTs apply the same intervention (with minor adaptations due to operational and contextual constraints) across different contexts and time windows (Milan in 2017, Turin in 2018, London in 2019).
decisions.reason: The shipped row mis-resolved 'Camuffo et al.' to Camuffo, Furlan, Romano, & Vinelli (2008), which is not cited anywhere in the paper, while attaching an outcome quote from this paper's abstract on idea termination and radical pivots. The primary text explicitly states that only one study had been published in this area and that the three new RCTs replicate Camuffo, Cordova, Gambardella, & Spina (2020) (blind target_index 0).

decisions.quote: Our results are generally consistent with Camuffo et al. (2020), which points to the robustness across contexts of the effects associated with the use of a scientific approach. Moreover, the large scale of our study allows us to detect effects non-detectable or negligible in smaller samples.
decisions.reason: Once the dependent original identity on row 1242 is resolved to Camuffo, Cordova, Gambardella, & Spina (2020), the authors' explicit overall replication verdict governs: they conclude that their results are generally consistent with Camuffo et al. (2020) and robust across contexts, while treating the stronger termination precision and nonlinear (focused) pivoting pattern in the larger sample as refinements enabled by scale.
